questions.question: Your team is building a pipeline that processes 50,000 scanned invoices per day. Most invoices are clean printed text, but about 10% contain handwritten notes or embedded charts. What is the most cost-effective architecture?
options: Send every invoice page through a vision model to ensure consistent extraction quality
Use OCR for all pages since it is cheaper, and accept lower accuracy on the handwritten and chart pages
Route clean text pages through OCR and route pages with handwriting or charts to a vision model
Transcribe each invoice with audio transcription, then process the transcript
questions.explanation: Routing by modality complexity is the right pattern: OCR handles clean printed text cheaply and accurately, while vision models handle the 10% of pages where layout, handwriting, or visual content matters. Sending all 50,000 pages through a vision model would cost 10x more for no improvement on the clean majority. OCR-only loses accuracy on the cases that specifically need vision. Audio transcription is not relevant to document images.

questions.question: A user uploads a PDF to your document Q&A system. Your pipeline extracts text with OCR, passes it through your input filters, then answers questions. A security researcher reports that a malicious image embedded in page 3 caused the system to output sensitive internal instructions. What happened?
options: The OCR step was misconfigured and extracted text from the image instead of ignoring it
The PDF parser exposed the raw image bytes to the model, bypassing OCR entirely
The vision model read adversarial text from the embedded image that OCR missed, and the model acted on those instructions
The input filters failed to catch a text-based injection in the OCR output
questions.explanation: This is a cross-modal prompt injection: the image contains text (possibly low-contrast or styled to evade OCR) that a vision model reads as instructions. Because the text-based input filters only saw the OCR output — which missed the image text — the adversarial instructions bypassed all defenses. OCR is not a sanitizer for vision model inputs. Any pipeline that accepts documents and processes images with a vision model must treat image-derived content as untrusted, just like user-submitted text.

questions.question: You are building a customer support system that handles audio call recordings. You need to extract the customer's stated issue and classify it by category. Which architecture is most appropriate for production today?
options: Send the raw audio directly to a vision-language model with a classification prompt
Transcribe the audio with a dedicated speech-to-text model, then classify the transcript with a text LLM
Use a multimodal embedding model to embed the audio and retrieve the closest category from a vector database
Convert the audio waveform to a spectrogram image and send it to a vision model
questions.explanation: The transcription pipeline (audio → text → LLM) is the production-standard approach for the vast majority of audio classification tasks. It gives you an auditable transcript as an artifact, lets you use any text-based model for classification, and is cheaper than native audio input. Native audio-in models exist but are not yet the default choice for production classification pipelines. Spectrogram images would lose semantic content that transcription preserves.

questions.question: You are estimating the monthly API cost for a pipeline that processes 5,000 product images per day, sending each image to a vision model with a short text prompt. You benchmark one image call at $0.004. Your estimate is 5,000 × $0.004 × 30 = $600/month. A colleague says the real cost will be higher. Why?
options: Vision API calls are billed per image, not per token, so the formula should use a higher per-image rate
High-resolution images tokenize into thousands of tile-tokens each, so larger images cost proportionally more — your benchmark image may have been small
The model charges extra for images that contain human faces due to privacy processing overhead
Vision models require more GPU memory, so the provider charges a memory surcharge on top of token costs
questions.explanation: Image cost scales with resolution because providers tile images into fixed-size chunks and charge per tile. A 512×512 benchmark image and a 2048×2048 product photo are not the same cost — the high-res image may generate 16x more tile-tokens. Your benchmark must use representative images from your actual dataset. Memory surcharges and face-detection fees are not standard billing mechanisms; the cost model is token-based, just with image-derived tokens.

questions.question: A vision model in your pipeline is performing poorly on a proprietary CAD diagram format your team uses internally. The same model handles standard architecture diagrams well. What best explains this and what should you do?
options: The model's image encoder has a bug with vector graphics — switch to a raster PNG export
CAD files require lossless compression — re-export at higher DPI to improve accuracy

The model's visual understanding is limited to patterns seen in training data; a diagram type absent from training will have degraded performance. Fine-tuning or adding textual annotation to the images is the mitigation.
Multimodal models cannot process engineering diagrams — use OCR to extract the dimension annotations instead
questions.explanation: Vision models learn visual patterns from training data. A proprietary CAD format that was not represented in training will produce unreliable outputs — not because the model is broken, but because it has no learned representation for that diagram type. The practical mitigations are: add descriptive text labels to the diagrams before sending them (annotating what each element means), or fine-tune the model on representative examples. DPI and compression format are rarely the cause of semantic understanding failures.
